fullPassage: More often than not, decision-making involves observing the choices of others. A team of researchers conducted an experiment to see how the hesitation of others in decision-making can affect an individual’s choice in a group setting. The participants sat at computers that displayed the same virtual bag filled with three balls, marked with either the letter “A” or “B.” They took turns pulling out one ball and guessing whether the bag contained more “A” or “B” balls. They could see the guesses made by those who went before them but couldn’t see the actual letters on the earlier balls. The results showed that participants were twice as likely to make a different guess if the previous participants exhibited reluctance in making their guess. This hesitancy was perceived as a lack of confidence, which prompted subsequent participants to disregard the previous choices of the group. Instead, they made guesses based on their own information —the letter on the ball they pulled. These findings suggest that reluctance in decision-making can interfere with groupthink and allow for a more individualized decision-making process.
